opus-5.5.text:
Well, the Earth is a sphere, and that sounds obvious, but a lot of early deep learning approaches to weather treated the atmosphere as a flat image. You take latitude-longitude data, lay it out as a rectangular grid, and run a standard convolutional network or vision transformer over it. The problem is that this grid is badly distorted. Near the poles, the grid points bunch together, so you're massively oversampling those regions, and at the edges of the map you get artificial boundaries that don't exist in reality. The atmosphere doesn't stop at the date line. It wraps around.

When you're doing a single-step prediction, these artifacts might seem small. But weather forecasting, and especially climate modeling, means rolling the model out autoregressively for hundreds or thousands of steps. Small errors from the wrong geometry compound. You see energy pile up at the poles, spurious high-frequency noise, and eventually the rollout blows up and becomes physically meaningless.

So with the Spherical Fourier Neural Operator, the idea was to respect the true geometry of the problem. Instead of an ordinary Fourier transform, which assumes a flat periodic domain, we use spherical harmonics, the natural basis for functions on a sphere. That gives us rotational equivariance and gets rid of the pole and boundary artifacts. Because it's a neural operator, it learns the mapping between functions rather than fixed grids, so it's not tied to one resolution.

The result was much more stable long-range rollouts. We could run the model for a year of simulated time and it stayed physically plausible, with realistic energy spectra, which matters a lot if you eventually want ensembles and climate-scale simulations. It's also extremely fast, orders of magnitude faster than traditional numerical weather prediction, so you can generate huge ensembles cheaply and get much better uncertainty estimates.

The broader lesson, which I come back to a lot, is that you shouldn't throw away domain knowledge just because you have a big neural network. When you build the right structure into the architecture, here the geometry of the domain, you get models that are more accurate, more data-efficient, and more trustworthy when you push them beyond the training regime.

r001.rationale: The response says spherical geometry led to “much more stable long-range rollouts” and that the model ran for a year of simulated time while remaining physically plausible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that the Earth is a sphere, and the model should know that.

When we built FourCastNet, the first version, we used Fourier neural operators. Those work on a flat, periodic grid. You take the global weather data, which comes on a latitude-longitude grid, and you treat it like a rectangle. That works surprisingly well, but it has a fundamental problem. A rectangle is not a sphere. The top and bottom edges of that rectangle are the poles, and on a real sphere the pole is a single point, not a line. Longitude lines converge there. So when you flatten the planet, you introduce artifacts, especially near the poles, and those errors compound as you roll the model forward in time.

That compounding is the real issue. For a two-day forecast you might get away with it. But we wanted long rollouts, weeks, and eventually we were looking at a year or more for climate-scale questions. Over those horizons, small inconsistencies at the boundaries grow into instabilities. The model would develop these unphysical patterns and eventually blow up.

So we asked, what is the natural generalization of the Fourier transform to the sphere? And that is the spherical harmonic transform. It is the right basis for functions on a sphere, the same way sines and cosines are the right basis for functions on a periodic interval. Meteorologists have known this for decades. Many of the operational numerical weather models are spectral models that use spherical harmonics. So we were really borrowing from that tradition and bringing it into the neural operator framework.

That gave us Spherical Fourier Neural Operators. The convolution is now done in the spherical harmonic domain, so the model respects the rotational symmetry of the globe. The poles are treated correctly. There are no seams. And the result was that we could run the model autonomously for a full year of simulated time and it stayed stable and physically plausible, which was not something the flat version could do.

There is a broader principle here that I care about a lot. Neural operators are about learning mappings between function spaces, not just between fixed grids of numbers. If you take that seriously, you have to respect the geometry of the domain the functions live on. The sphere is just the most obvious case for Earth science. But the same reasoning applies to other geometries in fluid dynamics, materials, and so on. Building the right structure into the model is far more effective than hoping the network discovers it from data.

r001.rationale: It says the spherical model stayed stable for a full year of simulated time and contrasts this with the flat model’s instability on long rollouts.

astra-6.text:
Because weather happens on a sphere, and we wanted the model to respect that geometry. If you flatten the Earth onto a rectangular grid, you introduce distortions, especially near the poles. Points that look far apart on that grid may actually be close together on the globe.

By incorporating spherical geometry, we give the model a representation that better matches the physical domain. That helps it capture how weather patterns interact across the planet without having to learn around artifacts of the coordinate system.

r001.rationale: The response explains that spherical geometry better matches Earth and avoids grid distortions, but it does not say this enabled longer forecast rollouts.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the Earth is a sphere, and that geometry matters when you’re trying to predict weather globally. If you treat the surface as a flat grid, you introduce distortions, especially near the poles, and artificial boundaries that the atmosphere doesn’t actually have.

So we wanted to build that geometry into the model. With spherical harmonics, we can represent patterns directly on the sphere and capture how weather systems interact across the globe. That gives the model a more appropriate foundation for learning atmospheric dynamics, which is particularly important when you keep rolling predictions forward over time.
